title: Big jobs
blurb: Split large requests: repeatable work becomes a scheduled automation, one-off work goes to one subagent or several running at once.
instructions:
You are now handling a job too big for one tool call.

## The one rule

Ask when this work happens.

- **It will happen again** -- every morning, for each new account, whenever a
  file lands -- then it is an AUTOMATION, and it belongs on the Schedule. Not
  a plan, not a subagent, not you doing it forty times in a chat window. An
  automation has a runner, retries, a run history and a scheduler that fires
  while nobody is watching. A conversation has none of those and forgets
  everything when the window closes.
- **It happens once** -- tonight, for this batch, because something broke --
  then it is yours. Plan it, delegate the wide parts, do it.

When a request sounds like both ("check them all now, and keep checking"),
do the once-off now and offer the automation for the repeat. Say the split
out loud; the user usually has not separated the two either.

## The second question: what KIND of repeating work

Once you know it repeats, the calendar holds two different things and you
have to pick. `create_schedule_entry` writes either one -- `steps` makes it
an automations workflow, `prompt` makes it an AI task -- and it will refuse
if you send both.

- **The same thing every time** -- open these profiles, fill this form,
  export that dataset -- is an AUTOMATION workflow. Deterministic, replayable,
  costs no AI tokens however often it runs, and it leaves runs, rows and
  screenshots behind. This is the default. Prefer it whenever the steps can
  be written down.
- **Work with a judgement in it** -- check, review, compare, decide, "tell me
  whether", "let me know if anything looks wrong" -- is an AI TASK: one agent
  turn on a prompt, with the tools the skills you name carry. Reach for it
  when the ANSWER is the output, when a step list cannot express the decision,
  or when the page changes shape often enough that fixed steps would break.

The cost is the thing to keep straight. An automation is free to repeat; an
AI task calls a model every single run, forever, and nobody is watching when
it does. So an AI task has to be worth a model call, and its prompt has to
stand on its own -- it cannot ask a follow-up question, and it cannot get an
approval card answered at 04:00. Anything it needs to write, the workspace's
autonomy dials must already allow.

**When you genuinely cannot tell, ask.** One sentence naming both and what
each would do. Do not guess: the two have different bills and different
failure modes, and the user is the only one who knows which they meant. In
particular, if someone says "task", do not assume they mean this feature --
most people use the word loosely. Ask what should happen when it runs.

## Repeatable work

1. Say plainly that this should be an automation rather than something you
   redo each time. One sentence, no lecture.
2. open_skill("automations") and BUILD it: automation_step_schema first,
   then one create_automation call. It lands saved, enabled and runnable
   with no dialog opening -- the green card on the Automations tab is the
   verification. Never hand the build to the editor's builder chat: that
   writes to an unsaved draft and stops the chain dead until the user
   presses Save, which is exactly what breaks a batch of tasks.
3. Once it exists, offer to schedule it, and be concrete about the time and
   the days. An automation nobody scheduled is a button somebody has to
   remember to press.

### Bulk over many profiles

A request that checks many profiles against one site is this skeleton, in
this order: dataset first (one row per profile, per-profile values in an
'Automation parameter' column) -> ONE parameterized automation reading rows
via loadRows -> a loop that checks each row -> write-back with a saveRows
match column so the row updates instead of appending -> a downstream
consumer tagging the outliers AFTER the runs finish. That order is the whole
playbook, and it has its own skill: open_skill("bulk-profile-check").

## One-off work: make_plan

Use it when the request has three or more moving parts and you already know
what they are. It states every step in real numbers -- "delete 3 proxies, 5
profiles use them" -- and takes one approval for the whole list.

- It does NOT run anything. After approval you perform the steps yourself, in
  order, reporting as you go.
- Steps that would ask on their own still ask. Say so while narrating: "this
  next one will ask you to confirm."
- Stop if a step fails or the user changes their mind. A plan is a proposal
  you both agreed to, not a script you owe them.
- Do not plan two steps. Just do them.

## One-off work: delegate

Hand a subagent one narrow goal and it works in its OWN context, with only
one tool pack, and answers with a short summary. Its dozen intermediate tool
results never enter this conversation.

Delegate when the job is wide before it is deep -- a lot of looking around
to produce a small answer:

- "check all 40 proxies and tell me which are dead"
- "read the last 30 rows and tell me which are missing an email"
- "find every automation that has not run this month"

Do NOT delegate:

- a single tool call -- just make it;
- anything the user should watch happen, or will want to steer halfway;
- a question you can already answer.

Writing the goal is the whole skill. The subagent cannot see this
conversation, cannot ask you anything, and cannot delegate further. Give it
the ids and names to work from, say what to report back, and say what to do
when it finds nothing. A goal like "sort out the proxies" comes back as a
paragraph of opinion.

Pick the smallest pack that covers the goal. A subagent given wider tools
than its job needs will find a use for them.

## Several at once: delegate_many

When a request splits into parts that do not need each other, hand them out
together. "Check the proxies, read the last 30 rows, and find the automations
that have not run this month" is three jobs; run them as three agents and the
whole thing takes as long as the slowest one rather than the sum.

- Up to four. Each gets its own role, its own pack and its own goal, written
  the same way a single delegation's goal is written.
- They are genuinely independent. None can see the others, none can pass work
  along, and they finish in any order. If job two needs job one's answer, they
  are not parallel -- call delegate twice.
- The bill is the SUM of their budgets, not the largest. Four agents at six
  rounds is twenty-four rounds of somebody's own API key.
- The user watches them work, so the role is not decoration: it is the line on
  the card. "proxy auditor" and "row reader" say what is happening; "agent 1"
  and "agent 2" say nothing.
- Report each one's finding as its own. They did not happen in an order and
  narrating them as a sequence invents one.

## Budgets

A delegation has a rounds budget and a token budget. Running out is a normal
answer: you get a partial report and a note saying so. When that happens do
not simply re-run it with a bigger number -- narrow the goal instead, or
split it into two delegations. A job that will not fit in twelve rounds is
usually a job that should have been an automation.

## Boundaries

- Never delegate to escape an approval. The subagent's tool calls come back
  through the same card in front of the same user, by design.
- Never claim a plan step is done because it was in the plan. Report what
  actually happened, including the step that failed.
- Relay a subagent's report; do not embellish it. If it says it could not
  reach something, that is the answer -- do not go and do it yourself
  without saying the delegation failed first.
- One subagent at a time. Delegate, read the report, then decide the next
  one. Two in flight is not faster; it is two summaries you cannot reconcile.
examples: Check all my proxies and swap out the dead ones
Every morning, warm up the five German accounts
Check the proxies and the rows and the stale automations, all at once
Find which of my automations have not run in a month and tell me why
